tasks.spec: You are reviewing an architecture, not fixing a bug. BOUNDARY: read only inside your own task directory; everything is staged in ./source/. Never modify anything outside your task directory, never call an API, never send a message. You own exactly one output file: ./report.md. THE SITUATION: an SMS agent books eye exams for an optometry practice. It has been patched four times in one evening, each time against whatever symptom the owner last reported, and it still fails. The owner's own diagnosis is that this has been local optimisation instead of architecture, and he is right. Your job is to do what those four patches did not. READ ./source/ARCHITECTURE-BRIEF.md FIRST AND COMPLETELY. It contains three live failures with the actual captured variables, every measured platform constraint, the measured gateway contract, and the non-negotiable safety constraints. Every measurement in it was executed against the live system. Treat them as fixed facts: you cannot take new measurements, and a design that contradicts a measured constraint is worthless. Then read ./source/v49_graph.json, the current live graph with every node, prompt, routing condition and response mapping, and ./source/build_v49.py which generates it. THE CENTRAL TENSION you must resolve: the language model is the ONLY component that can read a patient's intent, and it is the LEAST reliable component to carry structured data. Three times now, asking it to carry data across a boundary has produced partial or wrong values, and an empty value is fatal because the platform turns it into a JSON null the gateway rejects. Meanwhile the platform cannot filter, cannot index from the end of a list, cannot combine two routing conditions, and cannot compare one variable to another. WHAT TO DELIVER: (1) A judgement on whether the three failures in the brief share one root cause, and name it precisely. (2) The minimum a model must carry across a boundary for a booking to be safe on this platform, and whether that minimum can be reduced to something a small model gets right every time. Consider carrying an ordinal or a label rather than field values, and say what each option costs. (3) Where intent interpretation should live, and what the model should be prevented from deciding. (4) How the search window should be scoped and re-scoped as a conversation moves, given that the window is currently fixed by the patient's first message and never widens. (5) Whether the current node graph is the right shape at all, or whether a different decomposition would remove whole classes of failure rather than instances of them. (6) An explicit list of what your design does NOT fix and what it depends on someone else fixing. OUTPUT CONTRACT for ./report.md: start with '# Architecture Review'. Include '## Summary' with at most 3 bullets, then '## Findings', then '## Clean', then '## Assumptions'. Each finding uses exactly: '### Finding: <one line>' then 'Evidence:' citing a node id, a captured variable, or a measured constraint, 'Impact:' in terms of what a patient experiences, 'Fix:' concrete enough to implement, 'Priority: P0|P1|P2|P3', 'Confidence: high|medium|low'. Cite real node ids from the graph. Then a section '## Recommended Architecture' describing the shape you would build, node by node, naming what each node decides and what it is forbidden from deciding. Then '## Migration' giving the order of changes so the system is never left in a worse state than it is now. Then '## Not Fixed By This' listing the residual risks and external dependencies. HARD RULES: never invent a node id, a platform capability, or a gateway field. Do not propose anything the brief measured as unsupported. Do not propose prompt-tightening as a primary fix, since three rounds of it are already documented as insufficient. If you conclude the architecture is fundamentally unsuited to the platform, say so plainly and say what you would do instead. Under 2500 words.
tasks.verified: report.md has all required sections plus a recommended architecture and a migration order, cites at least 6 real node ids, invents none, and every finding carries evidence, impact, fix, priority and confidence

tasks.spec: You are designing the single most failure-prone interface in a live system. BOUNDARY: read only inside your own task directory; everything is staged in ./source/. Never modify anything outside your task directory, never call an API. You own exactly one output file: ./report.md. THE PROBLEM, narrowly: on a conversational-pathway platform, a small language model must hand a chosen appointment to a booking webhook. Three separate attempts have failed. Most recently the model was asked to copy a start time, an end time and a doctor id out of a list it had been shown; it copied the start time correctly and left the other two empty, the payload carried nulls, the gateway rejected it, and a real patient was told scheduling was unavailable. Earlier, five preference fields were captured and two received values belonging in other fields. READ ./source/ARCHITECTURE-BRIEF.md FIRST for the exact captured variables, the measured platform capabilities and the measured gateway contract. Also read ./source/v49_graph.json for how the current offer, verify and book nodes are wired, in particular n_offer, n_verify and n_book. YOUR JOB: design the narrowest possible contract between the model and the booking path, such that a small model cannot break it. Work through and cost out at least these options, plus any better one you find: carrying all payload fields as the model copies them, which is the current failing design; carrying a single ordinal such as which numbered option was chosen, and resolving the fields from a fixed position; carrying a single opaque token the gateway itself minted for each slot, if the response could supply one; carrying nothing at all and constraining the offer so the choice is always positional; and any scheme where a wrong or missing value fails closed rather than reaching the gateway as a null. For each option state exactly what the model must produce, what happens when it produces nothing, what happens when it produces something wrong, whether a booking could ever be written for a time the patient did not choose, and how it would be tested. Then commit to one recommendation and defend it. Pay particular attention to the failure mode where the model offers one time in the message and a different time reaches the payload, because that books a patient at a time they did not agree to and is the worst outcome available. OUTPUT CONTRACT for ./report.md: start with '# Capture Contract'. Include '## Summary' with at most 3 bullets, then '## Findings', then '## Clean', then '## Assumptions'. Each finding uses exactly: '### Finding: <one line>' then 'Evidence:', 'Impact:', 'Fix:', 'Priority: P0|P1|P2|P3', 'Confidence: high|medium|low'. Cite real node ids. Then '## Recommended Contract' stating precisely what the model produces, what the graph does with it, and the exact routing conditions that enforce it using only equality and inequality against string literals, since the platform supports nothing else. Then '## Proof' giving the executable test that would demonstrate a booking can never be written for a time the patient did not choose. HARD RULES: never invent a platform capability or a gateway field; the brief lists what is supported and what is not. Do not rely on prompt wording as the primary guarantee. Under 2000 words.
tasks.verified: report.md has all sections plus a recommended contract expressed in supported routing conditions and an executable proof, cites at least 5 real node ids, invents nothing

tasks.spec: You are mapping what patients actually ask for against what the system can currently do. BOUNDARY: read only inside your own task directory; everything is staged in ./source/. Never modify anything outside your task directory, never call an API. You own exactly one output file: ./report.md. READ ./source/ARCHITECTURE-BRIEF.md for the measured constraints and the live failures, ./source/v49_graph.json for the current graph, and ./source/scenarios.py for the 30 test cases the system is checked against today. YOUR JOB: enumerate the distinct things a patient can be asking for when they reply to an appointment offer, and for each one say whether the current graph can serve it, and if not, what specifically is missing. Work from real message behaviour, not categories: a day with no time; a time with no day; a part of the day; after or before an hour; the earliest available; the latest available; something later than a time already offered; something earlier than a time already offered; a different day entirely; any day at all as long as the time suits; two candidate days; a day the practice is closed; a date further out than the search window; changing their mind after choosing; asking what is available without committing; asking how busy a day is. For each: name the node that would handle it, the variables that would carry it, and the exact point where it breaks if it does. Then identify which of these the 30 existing scenarios already cover and which are untested, since an untested intent is where the next live failure will come from. OUTPUT CONTRACT for ./report.md: start with '# Intent Coverage'. Include '## Summary' with at most 3 bullets, then '## Findings', then '## Clean', then '## Assumptions'. Each finding uses exactly: '### Finding: <one line>' then 'Evidence:' citing a node id, a variable or a scenario name, 'Impact:', 'Fix:', 'Priority: P0|P1|P2|P3', 'Confidence: high|medium|low'. Cite real node ids from the graph. Include a table of every intent against covered-or-not and served-or-not. HARD RULES: never invent a node id, a variable name or a scenario name. Anything you cannot verify goes under Assumptions. Under 1800 words.
tasks.verified: report.md has all sections plus an intent coverage table, cites at least 6 real node ids, invents none, every finding carries the required fields
